text: '-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----Hash: SHA1==============================================================                    I\'m not really concerned with performance.                              -- SambaXP 07 Attendee referring                                           to LDAP Directories==============================================================Release Announcements=====================This is the third release candidate of the Samba 3.0.25 code baseand is provided for testing only.  An RC release means that we areclose to the final release but the code may still have a fewremaining minor bugs.  This release is *not* intended for productionservers.  There has been a substantial amount of development sincethe 3.0.23/3.0.24 series of stable releases.  We would like to ask theSamba community for help in testing these changes as we work towardsthe next significant production upgrade Samba 3.0 release.Major features included in the 3.0.25 code base include:  o Significant improvements in the winbind off-line logon support.  o Support for secure DDNS updates as part of the \'net ads join\'    process.  o Rewritten IdMap interface which allows for TTL based caching and    per domain backends.  o New plug-in interface for the \"winbind nss info\" parameter.  o New file change notify subsystem which is able to make use of    inotify on Linux.  o Support for passing Windows security descriptors to a VFS    plug-in allowing for multiple Unix ACL implements to running side    by side on the Same server.  o Improved compatibility with Windows Vista clients including    improved read performance with Linux servers.  o Man pages for IdMap and VFS plug-ins.Off-line Logons and AD Site Support===================================Winbind\'s capability to support offline logons has been greatlyimproved with the 3.0.25 release including support for locatingdomain controllers asynchronously using Active Directory Siteinformation.New IdMap Interface for Winbindd================================The 3.0.25 release of Samba includes a rewritten IdMap interfacefor winbindd which replaces the \"idmap backend\" parameter.  Pleaserefer to the \"idmap domains\" description in the smb.conf(5) manpage for more details.Dynamic DNS Updates===================The \"net ads join\" command is now able to register the host\'s DNS Arecords with Windows 2000 SP4 and 2003 DNS servers.  Thisfeature must be enabled at compile time using the --with-dnsupdatewhen running the ./configure script.  There is also a related \"net adsdns\" command for refreshing a host\'s records which could be launchedfrom a dhcp client script when a new IP address is obtained.Support for Additional ACL Modules==================================Samba\'s POSIX ACL support has been moved inside of the VFS layerwhich means it is now possible to support multiple ACL implementationson the same server including NFSv4 and GPFS ACLs.VFS ReadAhead Plugin====================Windows Vista introduces pipe-lined read support for improvedperformance when transferring files.  The new vfs_readahead pluginallows Linux file servers to utilize additional Kernel buffersfor caching files in order to avoid Disk I/O wait time when servingVista clients.  If you experience poor read performance betweenLinux servers and Vista clients

spam: Baker & McKenzie
column3: has penned a highly misleading articlein the Bangkok press
column4: arguing that the Thai compulsory licenses areunlawful under the TRIPS Agreement.  Three access lawyers refute theircontentions point-by-point.World\'s \"Premiere\" Law Firm Goes to Bat for Abbott:  Specious Arguments onThailand\'s Compulsory LicensesProfessor Brook K. Baker
column5: Health GAP and Northeastern U. School of Law
column7: American University
column8: Judit Rius Sanjuan
column10: 2007Baker & McKenzie proclaims itself as the world\'s leading global law firm
column11: so it\'s no surprise that this 3400 attorney firm with $1.5 billion inannual billings would go to bat for another big enterprise
column13: now locked in an intense battle with Thailand over thelegality and propriety of a government use license issued forKaletra/Aluvia (lopinavir/ritonavir)
column17: Compulsory druglicenses violate world trade treaty
column21: and more likely for the benefit of its BigPharma clients including Abbott
column26: the Baker & McKenzie attorneys have purposefully misread andmisrepresented the WTO TRIPS Agreement and wrongfully concluded thatThailand\'s license are unlawful.The authors make four TRIPS-related arguments
column27: all of which mischaracterizethe law.Tungsuwan and McKay first challenge the proposition that Thailand isjustified in issuing compulsory licenses on the grounds that \"public healthinterest must come before commercial interests
column28: \" belittling those groundsas comparable to acquiring beds in private hospitals.  The authors arefully capable of reading Article 31 of the TRIPS Agreement
column29: which containsno express limitation whatsoever on the grounds upon which a compulsorylicense can be granted.  The primacy of public health and public health\'svalidity as a ground for licenses
column31: was confirmed in the Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and PublicHealth of Nov. 2001 especially in paragraph 5(b) which reads:  \"Each Memberhas the right to grant compulsory licenses and the freedom to determine thegrounds upon which such licenses are granted.\"  Thus
column32: if Thailand wants toconserve resources in its world renowned HIV/AIDS treatment program
column34: the two Baker & McKenzie lawyers argue that Thailand\'s government uselicenses are not for \"public
column35: non-commercial use\" because they have beengranted to the Government Pharmaceutical Organization
column36: a publicly ownedmanufacturer and drug distribution agency.  Since the license is allegedlynot for public
column38: the authors argue that Thailand wasrequired to negotiate on commercially reasonable terms with the patentholder before issuing the license and that it failed to do so.   In makingthis argument
column41: that prior negotiations arenot required for public
column42: commercial use licenses; they fail to acknowledge
column44: that Thailand had in fact engaged in fruitless discussions withpatent holders since 2005.Contrary to the authors\' argument
column46: non-commercial use\"language of Article 31(b) of the TRIPS Agreement is focused on the \"use\"made of the licensed product
column47: not who the manufacturer or distributor is.Here
column48: the use is clear - Thailand will only use the licensedlopinavir/ritonavir within its national public health insurance schemes.Indeed
column49: Abbott will retain its exclusive rights to sell in Thailand\'ssmall private sector where it can continue to charge its exorbitantmonopoly prices.   As apologists for Abbott
column50: the authors would have usbelieve that licensees such as the GPO cannot make medicines for profit(not true)
column51: or that it\'s cheating when a locally owned public manufacturermakes or imports a licensed product from abroad (nothing could be furtherfrom the truth).  The compulsory licensing provisions of Article 31 permitlicenses to be granted to public or private
column52: and domestic or foreignentities.The authors third argument is that the .05\% royalty rate is unlawfulbecause it is not adequate and because it does not take into account the\"economic value of the authorization.\"  The authors continue with atruthful observation that customary royalty are higher elsewhere.  While itis true that royalty must be set fairly
column53: TRIPS merely requires a reviewremedy if the patent holder feels the royalty is inadequate.  Section 51 ofthe Patent Act provides for such an appeal
column54: and in fact Thailand hasinvited Abbott to several meetings to discuss the royalty.  Instead ofappealing
column56: Abbott has now decided to boycott royalty rate settingdiscussions.The authors\' final argument about the \"individual merits\" of licenses isplainly preposterous.  Once again arguing that prior negotiations arerequired
column57: the high-powered lawyers argue that Thailand cannot consider anylicense on its individual merits if it has not engaged in \"priorconsultations with the affected party.\"  Contrary to their claim
column58: Thailandunsuccessfully engaged in such discussions for several years.  More to thepoint
column60: the TRIPS Agreement expressly permits issuance of licensesfor emergencies
column63: non-commercial usewithout prior negotiations (Article 31(b)).  Pursuant to this internationalstandard and in compliance with its own law
column65: the U.S. and its contractors routinely issuepublic
column66: non-commercial use licenses without prior notice or negotiation
column67: for example to military hardware patents for its favored defensecontractors Lockheed-Martin and Halliburton.These highly skilled lawyers are not stupid and they do know how to read.They must be well aware of the authoritative scholarly interpretations ofthe TRIPS Agreement
column68: which clearly do not support their specious arguments.However
column69: high fees can buy twisted logic.  Here
column70: the false argumentsthreaten to obscure the legality of Thailand\'s compulsory licenses and bynecessary extension threaten access to life saving medicines.  In the U.S.legal system
column71: we have sanctions for frivolous arguments.  Here the authorsare seeking to mislead the court of public opinion rather than a judicialtribunal.  That may make their offense even worse.Professor Brook K. Baker
column72: Health GAPNortheastern U. School of LawProgram on Human Rights and the Global Economy400 Huntington Ave.Boston
column75: 2007BY InvitationCompulsory drug licences violate world trade treatyPEERAPAN TUNGSUWAN and WILLIAMMCKAYWe are familiar with the controversy that has been swirling around theissue of compulsory licensing (CL) of patented pharmaceuticals in Thailand.The Public Health Ministry has issued a white paper called \"10 BurningIssues\"
column76: which is an apologia for CL. The ministry proclaims CL is \"a formof social movement that aims at improving access to essential medicines andthe health of people\".In spite of substantial increases in budget expenditure in other areas
column77: theministry justifies CL by asserting that patented pharmaceuticals are tooexpensive for the Thai budget. It proclaims that the \"public healthinterest must come before commercial interests\".With this line of reasoning
column78: the ministry might just as well announce thatit will be compulsorily acquiring beds in private hospitals. Private bedsare undoubtedly too expensive. Such an action would also improve access andplace public health before commercial interests.Perhaps sensing that it needs to find some additional rationale
column79: theministry also asserts that its CL is in \"full compliance with the Thainational and international framework\". In this context
column80: this means in fullcompliance with section 51 of the Thai Patents Act and Article 31 of theWorld Trade Organisation\'s Agreement On Trade Related Aspects ofIntellectual Property Rights (Trips).In reality
column81: we think the ministry has failed to comply with Trips in anumber of important respects. In this article we will explain why this isso. In the next article
column82: we will discuss what might be done about it.First
column83: we believe the ministry has failed to comply with Article 31(b) ofTrips because it did not have prior consultations with patent holders. Inour view
column84: the CLs in favour of the Government Pharmaceutical Organisation(GPO) are for commercial use
column85: not for \"public non-commercial use\" as thegovernment claims and as required by Article 31 (b).Second
column86: the ministry has failed to comply with Article 31(h) of Tripsbecause the royalty rates stipulated (0.05\% in every case) are not\"adequate\" and fail to take into account the \"economic value of theauthorisation\" (the CL).And third and most important
column87: the ministry has failed to comply withArticle 31(a) because it has not considered each case \"on its own merits\".Let\'s discuss each of these failures in more detail:Failure to Consult: Article 31(b) of Trips mandates prior consultationswith the patent holder except in cases of emergency or \"publicnon-commercial use\". The ministry does not claim there is an emergency.However
column88: it does assert that the CLs in favour of the GPO are for a\"non-commercial purpose\".We think the GPO\'s use of the CL will be for a commercial purpose. In fact
column89: Section 6(5) of the GPO Act states that the GPO carries on \"business\".Sections 34 and 35 reinforce this basic objective.For example
column90: legislators envisaged the organisation making a surplus andhaving an obligation to pay this surplus to the government. The GPO alsohas joint ventures with private pharmaceutical companies. In the past
column91: somewanted the GPO privatised.The GPO will be selling the products for which Thailand is issuing CLs. Theroyalty obligations are expressed as a percentage of the GPO\'s \"salevalue\". In short
column93: both in form andsubstance. They do not cease to be such simply because the GPO is owned bythe government.Contrary to what the Public Health Ministry asserts in its white paper
column94: Section 51 of the Patents Act is in fact silent on the issue of whetherthere ought to be prior consultations with the patent holder. However
column95: Article 31(b) of Trips does say negotiations are required if the CL isissued for commercial use
column96: and we think the ministry has failed to comply.Inadequate Royalty Rate: The royalty rate of 0.05\% of the GPO\'s sales valueis not \"adequate\" and does take into account the \"economic value\" of the CLas required by Article 31(h) of Trips. The sales value
column98: of each product varies. Prima facie
column99: one would expect thatthe royalty rates for each product should vary. But they do not. The rateis the same for all three products.There is some curious logic in the White Paper. The ministry asserts thatsince the GPO will charge high retail prices for the products
column100: royaltyrates paid to the patent holders should be low.The opposite conclusion is more apt. If prices are high
column101: royalty ratesought also to be high to provide adequate compensation to the patentholder. To make the royalty rate \"adequate\" within the meaning of Article31(h)
column102: authorities should assess what rate might be applicable if this wasa voluntary licensing situation
column103: not just a CL situation.In our experience
column104: rates in voluntary licensing situations would be muchhigher
column105: typically in the range of at least 5\% to 7.5 \%
column106: and quite possiblysubstantially more. In one recent case in South Africa
column107: a 5\% rate wasdetermined for an antiretroviral
column108: and that involved a licence to settle acompetition dispute. In short
column109: any adequate rate would be likely to be wayin excess of the derisory 0.05\% stipulated by the ministry.Failure to Consider Individual Merits: The ministry failed to comply withArticle 31(a) of Trips because it did not consider each case on \"itsindividual merits\". This is the most basic and fundamental of all of theministry\'s failures to comply.To consider any case on \"its individual merits\" by definition requiresprior consultations with the affected party. That party must be given theopportunity to make its case and provide relevant evidence. Theseprinciples resonate in provisions such as Article 41(3) of Trips
column110: whichsays: \"Decisions on the merits of the case shall be based only on evidencein respect of which parties were offered the opportunity to be heard.\"In the case of every announcement of a CL
column111: the ministry ignored theseprinciples. It deliberately decided not to hold prior consultations. Itseems the ministry had a preconceived view that any prior consultationswere unlikely to be productive as far as it was concerned.By stipulating a blanket
column112: uniform royalty rate of 0.05\% for each product
column113: the ministry also failed to consider the individual merits of the products.Had it done so and given the patent holders the opportunity to presenttheir cases
column114: it may have realised each product and each CL is different
column115: and accordingly the rates ought to have been different and more adequate.Trips is an international treaty to which Thailand is as signatory. Underthe new interim constitution
column116: Thailand has an obligation to comply with itsobligations under international treaties
column117: including Trips. We will explorethe legal implications of this obligation in our next article.Peerapan Tungsuwan is a partner at Baker & McKenzie. She can be reached atpeerapan.tungsuwan@bakernet.com. William McKay is a consultant with thefirm
column118: and can be reached at william.mckay@bakernet.com._______________________________________________Ip-health mailing listIp-health@lists.essential.org'

text: 'http://www.bangkokpost.com/260407_News/26Apr2007_news24.phpBangkok PostApril 26
spam: 2007*Article misleads in support of Big Pharma*Peerapan Tungsuwan and William McKay (Business Post
column3: April 23)misleadingly and incorrectly argue that Thailand\'s compulsory licensingactions violate World Trade Organisation rules.This comes as little surprise. The two work at the global law firm Baker& McKenzie
column4: which has a huge business representing Big Pharma. AmongBaker & McKenzie\'s clients is Abbott
column5: the drug multinational attemptingto blackmail Thailand by withdrawing drugs it has submitted formarketing approval in the country. Other clients include Aventis andBristol-Myers Squibb
column6: Pfizer and Eli Lilly.The lawyers\' arguments do not pass the laugh test.They argue that Thailand\'s action does not constitute \"publicnon-commercial use\" because the compulsory licence permits theGovernment Pharmaceutical Organisation (GPO)
column7: an arguably commercialorganisation
column8: to use the patents. That is irrelevant. The licences arefor government use - distribution through the public health sector -which is what matters.The United States
column10: routinely issues \"public non-commercialuse\" licences in the defence sector to clearly commercial ventures (likeBoeing and Lockheed Martin).They complain that Thailand\'s royalty rate is too low. They neglect tomention that the patent holders are free to appeal the royalty rates
column11: but have in fact been uninterested in negotiating or litigating overroyalties.And they contend that Thailand did not consider each licence on its ownmerits. They ignore the reasoned basis that the Thai government has setout for its decision in each case. They creatively interpret provisionsof WTO rules to suggest that governments must always enter negotiationsprior to issuing compulsory licences
column12: despite explicit language to thecontrary - and despite common practice in the United States andelsewhere
column13: where government-use licences are issued with no priornegotiations.Peerapan Tungsuwan and William McKay aim to confuse readers bymisleadingly citing international law with which few non-specialists arefamiliar. Had they disclosed their firm\'s ties to Big Pharma
column14: everythingwould have been much clearer.ROBERT WEISSMANDirector
column16: Washington DCPROFESSOR BROOK K BAKERHealth GAP
column18: Programme on HumanRights and the Global Economy
column20: Programme on Information Justice and IntellectualProperty
column22: Washington DCJUDIT RIUS SANJUANForeign law adviser
column26: 2007BY InvitationCompulsory drug licences violate world trade treatyPEERAPAN TUNGSUWAN and WILLIAMMCKAYWe are familiar with the controversy that has been swirling around theissue of compulsory licensing (CL) of patented pharmaceuticals in Thailand.The Public Health Ministry has issued a white paper called \"10 BurningIssues\"
column27: which is an apologia for CL. The ministry proclaims CL is \"a formof social movement that aims at improving access to essential medicines andthe health of people\".In spite of substantial increases in budget expenditure in other areas
column28: theministry justifies CL by asserting that patented pharmaceuticals are tooexpensive for the Thai budget. It proclaims that the \"public healthinterest must come before commercial interests\".With this line of reasoning
column29: the ministry might just as well announce thatit will be compulsorily acquiring beds in private hospitals. Private bedsare undoubtedly too expensive. Such an action would also improve access andplace public health before commercial interests.Perhaps sensing that it needs to find some additional rationale
column30: theministry also asserts that its CL is in \"full compliance with the Thainational and international framework\". In this context
column31: this means in fullcompliance with section 51 of the Thai Patents Act and Article 31 of theWorld Trade Organisation\'s Agreement On Trade Related Aspects ofIntellectual Property Rights (Trips).In reality
column32: we think the ministry has failed to comply with Trips in anumber of important respects. In this article we will explain why this isso. In the next article
column33: we will discuss what might be done about it.First
column34: we believe the ministry has failed to comply with Article 31(b) ofTrips because it did not have prior consultations with patent holders. Inour view
column35: the CLs in favour of the Government Pharmaceutical Organisation(GPO) are for commercial use
column36: not for \"public non-commercial use\" as thegovernment claims and as required by Article 31 (b).Second
column37: the ministry has failed to comply with Article 31(h) of Tripsbecause the royalty rates stipulated (0.05\% in every case) are not\"adequate\" and fail to take into account the \"economic value of theauthorisation\" (the CL).And third and most important
column38: the ministry has failed to comply withArticle 31(a) because it has not considered each case \"on its own merits\".Let\'s discuss each of these failures in more detail:Failure to Consult: Article 31(b) of Trips mandates prior consultationswith the patent holder except in cases of emergency or \"publicnon-commercial use\". The ministry does not claim there is an emergency.However
column39: it does assert that the CLs in favour of the GPO are for a\"non-commercial purpose\".We think the GPO\'s use of the CL will be for a commercial purpose. In fact
column40: Section 6(5) of the GPO Act states that the GPO carries on \"business\".Sections 34 and 35 reinforce this basic objective.For example
column41: legislators envisaged the organisation making a surplus andhaving an obligation to pay this surplus to the government. The GPO alsohas joint ventures with private pharmaceutical companies. In the past
column42: somewanted the GPO privatised.The GPO will be selling the products for which Thailand is issuing CLs. Theroyalty obligations are expressed as a percentage of the GPO\'s \"salevalue\". In short
column44: both in form andsubstance. They do not cease to be such simply because the GPO is owned bythe government.Contrary to what the Public Health Ministry asserts in its white paper
column45: Section 51 of the Patents Act is in fact silent on the issue of whetherthere ought to be prior consultations with the patent holder. However
column46: Article 31(b) of Trips does say negotiations are required if the CL isissued for commercial use
column47: and we think the ministry has failed to comply.Inadequate Royalty Rate: The royalty rate of 0.05\% of the GPO\'s sales valueis not \"adequate\" and does take into account the \"economic value\" of the CLas required by Article 31(h) of Trips. The sales value
column49: of each product varies. Prima facie
column50: one would expect thatthe royalty rates for each product should vary. But they do not. The rateis the same for all three products.There is some curious logic in the White Paper. The ministry asserts thatsince the GPO will charge high retail prices for the products
column51: royaltyrates paid to the patent holders should be low.The opposite conclusion is more apt. If prices are high
column52: royalty ratesought also to be high to provide adequate compensation to the patentholder. To make the royalty rate \"adequate\" within the meaning of Article31(h)
column53: authorities should assess what rate might be applicable if this wasa voluntary licensing situation
column54: not just a CL situation.In our experience
column55: rates in voluntary licensing situations would be muchhigher
column56: typically in the range of at least 5\% to 7.5 \%
column57: and quite possiblysubstantially more. In one recent case in South Africa
column58: a 5\% rate wasdetermined for an antiretroviral
column59: and that involved a licence to settle acompetition dispute. In short
column60: any adequate rate would be likely to be wayin excess of the derisory 0.05\% stipulated by the ministry.Failure to Consider Individual Merits: The ministry failed to comply withArticle 31(a) of Trips because it did not consider each case on \"itsindividual merits\". This is the most basic and fundamental of all of theministry\'s failures to comply.To consider any case on \"its individual merits\" by definition requiresprior consultations with the affected party. That party must be given theopportunity to make its case and provide relevant evidence. Theseprinciples resonate in provisions such as Article 41(3) of Trips
column61: whichsays: \"Decisions on the merits of the case shall be based only on evidencein respect of which parties were offered the opportunity to be heard.\"In the case of every announcement of a CL
column62: the ministry ignored theseprinciples. It deliberately decided not to hold prior consultations. Itseems the ministry had a preconceived view that any prior consultationswere unlikely to be productive as far as it was concerned.By stipulating a blanket
column63: uniform royalty rate of 0.05\% for each product
column64: the ministry also failed to consider the individual merits of the products.Had it done so and given the patent holders the opportunity to presenttheir cases
column65: it may have realised each product and each CL is different
column66: and accordingly the rates ought to have been different and more adequate.Trips is an international treaty to which Thailand is as signatory. Underthe new interim constitution
column67: Thailand has an obligation to comply with itsobligations under international treaties
column68: including Trips. We will explorethe legal implications of this obligation in our next article.Peerapan Tungsuwan is a partner at Baker & McKenzie. She can be reached atpeerapan.tungsuwan@bakernet.com. William McKay is a consultant with thefirm
column69: and can be reached at william.mckay@bakernet.com._______________________________________________Ip-health mailing listIp-health@lists.essential.org'

text: 'This is a multi-part message in MIME format.--[ Picked text/plain from multipart/alternative ]INDIANS WECOME MOVE TO OVERCOME PATENTS ON ESSENTIAL DRUGS IN THAILANDCOMPULSORY LICENSES NEEDED TO REDUCE PRICES OF ESSENTIAL DRUGSNew Delhi
spam: 26 April 2007 - The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+) and the Lawyers Collective HIV/AIDS Unit (LCHAU) today joined  public interest and health groups around the world to demonstrate their support for the actions of the Thai Government to increase access to essential medicines for their citizens.Since November 2006
column3: Thailand has issued compulsory licenses for three patented medicines
column4: including the AIDS drugs efavirenz and lopinavir/ritonavir. This procedure authorises the Thai health authorities to begin producing or importing affordable generic versions of the drugs
column5: which are patented in Thailand.Compulsory licenses are a legally recognised means to overcome barriers in accessing affordable medicines. \'The use of compulsory licenses to improve access to essential medicines is fully consistent with the World Trade Organization TRIPS Agreement
column6: which sets out the international rules on patents\'
column7: says Kajal Bhardwaj of the Lawyers Collective.In reaction to the Thai health authorities\' decision
column8: Abbott
column10: has decided not to bring to the Thai market any of its new medicines
column11: including a crucially important HIV/AIDS drug (heat-stable lopinavir/ritonavir).Indian organizations are strongly condemning Abbott\'s decision to pressurize the Thai government to withdraw the compulsory licenses. Loon Gangte from DNP+
column12: speaking at a rally held in Delhi said
column13: \'Abbott\'s action of holding the lives of Thai patients to ransom is unethical
column15: \'compulsory licenses on medicines are necessary when essential medicines
column17: are unavailable or unaffordable.\'Since the issuance of a compulsory license on the AIDS drug Efavirenz in November 2006
column18: the Thai Government has been able to buy generic versions of the drug at much lower prices and will be able to provide it to an additional 20
column19: 000 people in need.At the rally in New Delhi

column6: then the OS will start swappingmemory to disk
column7: but the OS does not know what parts of memory correspondto which objects
column8: so it is entirely possible that the chunk swapped todisk contains parts of different data objects
column9: so when you need one ofthose objects again
column10: everything needs to be swapped back in.  This isvery inefficient.S-PLUS occasionally runs into the same problem
column11: but since it does someof its own swapping to disk it can be more efficient by swapping singledata objects (data frames
column13: since S-PLUS is already savingeverything to disk
column14: it does not actually need to do a full swap
column15: it canjust look and see that a particular data frame has not been used for awhile
column16: know that it is already saved on the disk
column17: and unload it frommemory without having to write it to disk first.The g.data package for R has some of this functionality of keeping dataon the disk until needed.The better approach for large data sets is to only have some of the datain memory at a time and to automatically read just the parts that youneed.  So for big datasets it is recommended to have the actual datastored in a database and use one of the database connection packages toonly read in the subset that you need.  The SQLiteDF package for R isworking on automating this process for R.  There are also the bigdatamodule for S-PLUS and the biglm package for R have ways of doing some ofthe common analyses using chunks of data at a time.  This idea is notnew.  There was a program in the late 1970s and 80s called Rummage byDel Scott (I guess technically it still exists
column18: I have a copy on a 5.25\"floppy somewhere) that used the approach of specify the model you wantedto fit first
column19: then specify the data file.  Rummage would then figure outwhich sufficient statistics were needed and read the data in chunks
column20: compute the sufficient statistics on the fly
column21: and not keep more than acouple of lines of the data in memory at once.  Unfortunately it did nothave much of a user interface

text: 'James E Keenan wrote:> > Since November I\'ve been working on maintaining those of Parrot\'s > configuration and build tools written in Perl 5.  Lately I\'ve been > trying to recruit others to help in that process.  The discussion in > this thread suggests that at some future point some or all of the Perl > scripts/modules I\'ve been working on will be replaced with ... something > else.This has been the plan all along. column3: of course
column4: makes me wonder what I\'m doing now and
column6: makes me wonder what to say to other people with Perl 5 > skills who want to help with the Parrot project.Agile development in action. We can\'t know the full set of requirements for the build system until we have a working build system. And we can\'t delay all development waiting for the perfect build system. So we work in stages of refinement. Your work here is enormously helpful.> This is not simply an ego thing on my part.  I\'ve written very little of > the Perl 5 tools and taken on maintenance of a bit more
column7: but one thing I > realize is how much of Parrot\'s source code is written in Perl 5.  How > much of that must eventually be replaced?How much needs to be replaced depends on the strategy we take. One possibility is to take some of the core pieces
column8: make any minor modifications needed to run on Parrot\'s implementation of Perl 5
column10: and run them on miniparrot. There are advantages and disadvantages to a bootstrapping strategy like this
column11: it will work for some parts of the build system but not for others.Some parts of the build system can be run on the maintainer side rather than the user side. So
column12: the release manager and developers can have a dependency on Perl 5

column14: only those parts that are late enough to have a working miniparrot).> And who is going to maintain it? column15: we don\'t want to write an entire build system in C. It\'s a horrible language for the kinds of dynamic effects we need in the build system. Some parts will be in C

column3: so it can offer them to all Thai citizens

column5: which has put the country on a collision course with the bigpharmaceutical firms.Six years ago I visited a clinic outside Bangkok

column14: as they are provided by thegovernment\'s universal healthcare scheme or by HIV/Aids organisations.This is possible because of Thailand\'s decision to make cheap
column15: genericcopies of ARVs at a fraction of the cost of the branded drugs.It is something the big pharmaceutical companies resisted at first

text: 'Jonathan raised a question in the #parrotsketch meeting today about our strategy for safely changing classes that already have instantiated objects. The core problem is this: when you create a class
spam: .local pmc classobj
column3: object   classobj = newclass \'Foo\'instantiate an object from it
column4: object = classobj.\'new\'()and then modify the class
column6: $P3)- At that point you want \'object\' to still reference the old class
column7: so it can continue operating without disruption. No problem
column8: you just don\'t make any changes to it.- And we can create a new class object inside the add_method call and redispatch the add_method to it
column9: leaving the original class object unmodified.- The problem is that after the call you want the \'classobj\' variable to contain the new class
column10: rather than the old class. We don\'t have an effective way of morphing that variable to the new class from within a method call on that class. Or
column13: but only by altering the class itself
column14: which will morph all references to the class
column15: including the references from the instantiated objects (which should reference the old class instead).Some alternatives:1) Do away with safe morphing. Allow all dynamic changes to the class even after it has been instantiated. Flag in the class that it\'s been modified after instantiation

text: 'Matt Diephouse wrote:> > It looks like the PMC variant is correct in this case
spam: because Object> isn\'t actually a class. There\'s a class flag for PMCs that sets> whether or not they are a class and Object doesn\'t have this set.> > When you call the PMC variant of isa
column3: it calls Parrot_object_isa
column4: and> that has this code:> >    /* if this is not a class */>    if (!PObj_is_class_TEST(pmc)) {>        pmc = VTABLE_get_class(interp
column5: pmc);>    }> > So since Object isn\'t a class
column6: it calls the get_class vtable and gets> the Class pmc. It then tests the object to see if it\'s a Class
column7: which> it obviously isn\'t.You should always get the same answer from the \'isa\' opcode
column8: whether you pass in a string or a PMC. In this case
column9: object.pmc should override the \'isa\' vtable method to delegate the lookup to the object\'s class. (ParrotObject.pmc inherits an overridden \'isa\' from ParrotClass.pmc.)Ultimately
column10: both variants of the \'isa\' opcode should call the vtable \'isa\' (preserving encapsulation
column12: etc.) This means the vtable isa needs to be able to handle keyed lookup. (Unless we reverse the decision of RT#39045.)An object should never report that it \'isa\' Object
column13: it should only report an \'isa\' relationship to the classes it inherited from. (Different HLLs will have different notional hierarchies
column14: and we don\'t want Parrot\'s low-level implementation details to be visible in the mix.)'

text: 'The Schoenhage-Strassen O(n log n log log n) bound is obsolete: MartinFuerer
spam: in a paper \"Faster integer multiplication\" to appear at STOC2007
column3: has proven a bound of n (log n) 2^(log* n)
column4: where log* is thenumber of log iterations required to reach 1.This was stated as a purely asymptotic result
column5: and an improvement fromlog log n to 2^(log* n) might not sound noticeable for any reasonablevalue of n; but I think that Fuerer\'s idea is worth investigating formultiplications in practice.The core idea
column6: which I\'ll choose some concrete parameters to illustrate
column7: is to perform an FFT of size 1048576 over the ring \\C[x]/(x^16 + 1)
column8: using a 32768th root of x in the ring as the 1048576th root of 1. Thisinvolves   10485760 additions in the ring (so 335544320 additions in \\R)
column10: and   10485760 multiplications in the ring.You\'re supposed to know that---as in the split-radix FFT---you canarrange for most of the multiplications in an FFT to be by \"easy\" rootsof 1. In this case
column11: most of the multiplications are by powers of x
column13: with negations absorbed intosubsequent operations. A small fraction of the multiplications
column16: whichasymptotically should be embedded into smaller integer multiplications
column17: with precomputations on the constant inputs.Actually
column18: \\C is unnecessary. The ring \\R[x]/(x^16 + 1) has   sum_{j = -15
column23: eliminating roundoff error. If p has 56bits
column25: then additions mod p will simply be 64-bit machineadditions
column26: and multiplications in (\\Z/p)/(x^16 + 1) can be embedded intomultiplications mod 2^2048 + 1 with minimal overhead. The traditionalproblem with number-theoretic transforms
column27: namely the serious slowdown inmultiplications mod p
column28: is nicely addressed by Fuerer\'s user-selectablereduction in the frequency of multiplications.For comparison
column29: a normal size-16777216 FFT over \\C with the tangent FFT(Van Buskirk) would take   521957832 additions in \\R
column32: if I\'ve counted correctly. (A traditional split-radix FFT would take466033784 multiplications and the same number of additions/subtractions
column33: but would allow 113712244 multiplications to be replaced by additions;maybe a good tradeoff if multiplications are expensive.) A size-16777216FFT over \\R is about half the cost. Maybe 184 operations in \\R are lessexpensive than 1 multiplication in (\\Z/p)/(x^16 + 1)
column35: since most of the bits are lost to roundoff error.Going beyond 64-bit precision in \\R makes the multiplications much moreexpensive.---D. J. Bernstein

text: 'Hi
spam: there is currently no obvious way to explicitly set the winbind separator to \'\\\' in smb.conf. Even worse
column3: the default given in the man page of smb.conf is wrong:winbind separator = \'\\\'This will actually set the separator to a single quote (\'). Similarly
column4: winbind separator = \"\\\"will set it to a double quote (\"). People may also think thatwinbind separator = \\\\works. And yes
column6: but the next line in the config file will have no effect
column7: because it\'s taken as continuation of the winbind separator line.One way that works iswinbind separator = \\garbagebut imho this is not really obvious.Thus
column8: this should either either be fixed so that \'\\\' and \"\\\" both work as expected
column9: or the problem should be described in the man page!Comments

column3: but there was a secondary (and more subtle)  bug in ctdb that the bug in smbd exposed. When we get send a dmaster  reply

column8: Unusual\tpaintings are shipped from rural Croatia - a delicate art in itself.To: Museum Security Network Mailinglist <msn-list@te.verweg.com>Message-ID: <46358687.6080703@bruggemansolutions.com>Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8; format=flowedGallery owner has eye for \'naive\' art    Unusual paintings are shipped from rural Croatia - a delicate art in itself.By PAUL SWIDERPublished April 29
column9: 2007ST. PETERSBURG - After six months of flawless operation at his new gallery
column10: Jim Nannen\'s worst business fear came to pass: A shipment of fragile glass paintings worth $70
column11: 000 had gone missing somewhere in Europe.\"Nobody was able to give us a proper answer
column13: the owner of Croatian Naive Art Gallery on Beach Drive. \"When I went into this business
column14: this was my biggest concern.\"Nannen sells and displays artworks painted in reverse on glass. They come from a decades-old tradition of artists
column15: often referred to as amateur or naive artists
column16: who live in rural border regions of Croatia near Hungary. Because the paintings are relatively rare and delicate and come from a remote part of the world
column17: Nannen was always worried about transferring them from the Croatian countryside to the United States.This latest shipment was bundled up April 11 by a FedEx franchise in Zagreb
column18: the Croatian capital. It was supposed to reach Nannen
column19: as had all his previous packages
column20: in about three days. This was the largest and most valuable shipment to date.\"Once it left Zagreb
column22: \" Nannen said.Some reports had the 400-pound crate in Paris; others in Frankfurt. There were suggestions the package had been stolen
column23: and Interpol called the gallery about its investigations. There was even talk of getting the FBI involved. The story was picked up by the Zagreb media.Then on April 21
column24: Nannen got a call that the package was on its way to FedEx headquarters in Memphis
column25: Tenn. When it didn\'t arrive the next day
column26: he called and learned it hadn\'t been shipped to Tampa
column28: but was on its way to Seattle.FedEx spokesman Steve Barber did not have details about the specific shipment but he said the company\'s systems eventually worked. The shipment arrived on April 26. He said he\'s investigating whether FedEx will offer the gallery a discount for its troubles.Nannen was ill prepared for such international intrigue. He\'d spent his life running pet stores
column29: first in Massachusetts and then starting and growing the Animal House chain here. But he caught the art bug when he went to a Croatian art exhibit in 2000 at the Museum of Fine Arts. He was so captivated by the mood
column31: color and character of the naive art that he set about creating a collection.As he scoured the Internet for dealers
column32: Nannen learned that the art form was rare in the United States. He visited Croatia for an exhibit there and was driven to tour the country
column33: knocking on farmhouse doors searching for the farmer artists. Seeing a business opportunity
column34: he decided to start a U.S. gallery.The business now sits on the ground floor of Parkshore Plaza
column35: across from Straub Park. His pieces range from $300 to $400 for a postcard-size work to $30
column36: 000 for larger pieces.He has about 200 paintings on display
column37: but this latest shipment of 67 represented a significant new addition. \"I was concerned about how I was going to continue the business
column38: \" he said.Now that his box has arrived
column39: Nannen said he can sleep again.\"This is very different from the pet business.\"If you go:Croatian Naive Art Gallery300 Beach Drive NE824-2800http://www.sptimes.com/------------------------------Message: 2Date: Mon

column138: 30 Apr 2007 08:03:44 +0200From: Museum Security Network Mailing list <msn-list@te.verweg.com>Subject: [MSN] Currency caper at Bank of Canada leaves cash till shortTo: Museum Security Network Mailinglist <msn-list@te.verweg.com>Message-ID: <463586C0.8090903@bruggemansolutions.com>Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8; format=flowed*Currency caper at Bank of Canada leaves cash till short**By DEAN BEEBY*OTTAWA (CP) - Someone has helped themselves to a few choice specimens from the Bank of Canada\'s currency museum
column139: newly released documents show.Red-faced bank officials are short about $16
column140: 700 following the unsolved theft at the central bank\'s popular tourist attraction.\"There is no plausible explanation for the discrepancy other than theft
column141: \" says an internal audit obtained by The Canadian Press under the Access to Information Act.\"The procedures for note holdings should have been stronger . . . some of the procedures that did exist were not followed.\"The missing money came not from the display cases
column142: but disappeared from a stash of cash the museum uses to help teach visitors about counterfeit currency.The so-called note exchange program allowed patrons to swap their old-style bills for new-series money with special security features designed to thwart counterfeiters. The popular program
column144: has been abruptly cancelled in the wake of the currency caper.Bank officials first noticed money was missing in June last year
column145: but took five months to complete an audit and call in the Ottawa police
column146: internal documents show.Asked why the process took so long
column147: bank spokesman Christian Vezeau said only that \"we conducted a thorough internal investigation through which we were able to rule out any accounting errors and we concluded that the money was stolen.\"Det. Tracey Turpin of the Ottawa police said the case is now considered closed
column148: partly because the bank complained long after the alleged theft.\"A lot of time had passed and just about everybody that had worked at the time had moved on
column149: \" Turpin said in an interview. \"To track who was working when
column150: when the money would have gone missing
column151: was virtually impossible.\"The police did not conduct any interviews. But the Bank of Canada\'s own investigation suggested it was an inside job because the money went missing in an area accessible only to employees
column152: Turpin said.Vezeau declined to say whether any staff members have been disciplined or fired
column153: citing privacy rules.He added: \"The procedures in place for the storage
column154: handling and regular counting of the money for the boutique till were further tightened when the museum became aware of the shortage.\"The currency museum
column157: is nestled inside the original 1934 Bank of Canada building
column158: which itself is embedded inside the bank\'s modern glass-and-steel towers near Parliament Hill.Opened in 1980
column159: the modest facility costs about $1.5 million a year to operate
column160: with 20 full-time staff. There\'s no admission charge and guided tours are free. The galleries feature coins and currency from around the world
column161: with an emphasis on Canadian money.The internal audit
column163: noted that \"high staff turnover\" was partly responsible for the lax security that apparently allowed the theft. \"Management oversight in such an environment should have been stronger
column164: \" it said.The heist at headquarters is not the first time the central bank - which prides itself on tight security - has seen its assets go AWOL.In 2004
column165: a bank employee was fired and charged with theft after $10
column166: 000 was stolen from a Toronto bank-note facility
column167: where large bundles of cash are received from chartered banks.And in 2001
column168: the central bank lost track of $1 million worth of $1
column169: 000 notes at an Ottawa-area shredding facility. An exhaustive internal investigation found that \"misappropriation of bank notes cannot be conclusively ruled out

column4: and then use sweep to fill it out... Here\'s my code for the general solution...### FnInflate### ¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨¨#Inflates an input array of arbitray size along the necessary dimensions to achieve the#same size as that in target.dim#balloon    :   array to be \"inflated\"#target.dim :   final size of \"balloon\". NB target.dim and balloon must have the same NUMBER of dimensions...FnInflate     <-  function(balloon
column5: target.dim) {  #Check number of input dimensions  dim.balloon     <-  dim(balloon)  if(length(target.dim)!=length(dim.balloon)) {    stop(\"Input array does not have the same dimensionality as indicated in target.dim.\")  }  #Identify the dimensions along which to inflate the array  same.dims               <-  dim.balloon == target.dim             #A boolean array indicating whether the arrays correspond in that dimension  corresponding.dims      <-  (1:length(target.dim))[same.dims]     #Dimensions that correspond between the target dim and the input array  non.corresponding.dims  <-  (1:length(target.dim))[!same.dims]     #Dimensions that do not correspond between the target dim and the input array  #Check that the non-corresponding dimensions are all of size 1 in the input array - we don\'t know what to do if this is not the case  if(prod(dim(balloon)[non.corresponding.dims] == 1)==FALSE) {    stop(\"Input array not suitable for inflation as non-corresponding dimensions are not of size 1.\")  }  #Create temp array of 1s  inflated.balloon  <-  array(1
column6: dim=target.dim)  #And inflate using sweep  inflated.balloon  <-  sweep(inflated.balloon
column7: corresponding.dims

text: 'One problem you will have to face is that you have no control over theclients (on Windows or Linux) that use the SMB protocol to access filesand directories.  For example
spam: you will soon find that the clientsrequire you to return an accurate file byte size value
column3: and that someclients (e.g.
column4: Windows Explorer) ask for the file status informationover and over.  This isn\'t exactly a POSIX issue
column5: but it is aside-effect of the fact that POSIX makes asking for file statusinformation cheap.  If you can\'t map the incoming SMB functions tosimilarly cheap operations on your proprietary file system
column6: then youwill have a tough time having reasonable performance.But whether you implement the mapping from Samba to your FS by emulatinga POSIX environment or by writing a VFS layer
column7: it can be done.  As awild guess
column8: you are looking at writing a few thousand lines of code.'

column7: but     prototypes that are sent abroad...templates or blueprints or any other     idea that gets sent abroad that needs to be combined with something     physical in order to potentially infringe.\"   In this case \"gold master\" CDs of Microsoft software are sent abroad where copies are made and installed on hardware.  The US court is suggesting that software patents only apply when they are combined with hardware (that whole \"new machine\" legal theory I saw in CIPO\'s new MOPOP)
column8: and are not infringing when they are only in intangible form (IE: software ideas on a CD).   An interesting question: if patentable software is combined with hardware in a jurisdiction that doesn\'t honour bogus software patents (I consider all information/mental process patents to be bogus)

column3: rip out the old implementation

column6: or we can refactor the existing ops and supporting code to support the old and new metamodels
column7: and when both are passing all the tests

column9: my preference is the refactor approach. We need to support multiple class/object implementations anyway. Refactoring to support the two we have now moves us closer to our goals than simply replacing the old implementation. Running two implementations will also force us to respect encapsulation boundaries much more than the current implementation does.Any concerns? column10: the U.S. patent systemwill undergo its most substantial overhaul since Congress passed thePatent Act in 1952.The Reform Act will affect virtually every facet of the patentprocess. Key features proposed in the bill include:     * Transitioning to a \"first to file\" system (35 U.S.C. § 102).     * Eliminating interference proceedings and institutingderivation proceedings (35 U.S.C. § 135).     * Permitting the filing of a substitute statement in lieu ofexecuting an inventor\'s oath or declaration (35 U.S.C. § 115).     * Permitting assignees to file applications in their own names(35 U.S.C. § 118).     * Enumerating a damages analysis whereby the court determinesthat a reasonable royalty is applied only to that economic valueproperly attributable to the patentee\'s specific improvement over theprior art (35 U.S.C. § 284).     * Describing a damages analysis that provides

text: 'Before you go down that road
spam: I would recommend first seeing if it is  really a problem. Premature code optimization is in my opinion never  a good idea.Also
column3: reading the Details on ?attach you will find this:\tThe database is not actually attached. Rather
column4: a new environment is  created on the search path and the elements of a list (including  columns of a data frame) or objects in a save file or an environment  are copied into the new environment. If you use <<- or assign to  assign to an attached database
column5: you only alter the attached copy
column6: not  the original object. (Normal assignment will place a modified version  in the user\'s workspace: see the examples.) For this reason attach  can lead to confusion.So in fact it is the attaching that has to do copying
column7: not the other  way around.As for references
column8: perhaps there is a better one
column9: but searching for  \"pass\" in \"Writing R Extensions\" I found the following on page 41:\tSome memory allocation is obvious in interpreted code
column11: y <- x + 1allocates memory for a new vector y. Other memory allocation is less  obvious and occurs becauseR is forced to make good on its promise of ?call-by-value? argument  passing. When an argumentis passed to a function it is not immediately copied. Copying occurs  (if necessary) only whenthe argument is modified. This can lead to surprising memory use.Perhaps a better source

text: 'Right: SAS objects (at least in the base and statistics components of the system -- there are dozens of add-ons for particular markets) are simple databases.  the predominant model for data manipulation and statistical calculation is a row by row operation that creates modified rows and/or accumulates totals.  This was pretty much the only way things could be done in the days when real (and typically virtual) memory was much smaller than it now is.  It can be a pretty efficient model for calculatons that fit that pattern.  One downside of course is that a line of R code can easily turn into 30 lines of SAS with data steps

The storage of the object would be handled by a database and there would have to be an efficient interface for pulling a row (or small chunk of rows) out of the database repeatedly; alternatively the operatons could be conducted insidethe database.  Basic operations of rowwise calculation and cumulation(such as forming a column sum or a sum of outer-products) would bewritten in an R-like syntax and translated into an efficient set ofoperations that work through the database. column4: SAS is more efficient handling large data > > probably than S+/R. Do you have any idea why?> > SAS originated at a time when large data sets were stored on > magnetic tape and the only reasonable way to process them was > sequentially.> Thus most statistics procedures in SAS act as filters
column5: > processing one record at a time and accumulating summary > information.  In the past SAS performed a least squares fit > by accumulating the crossproduct of [X:y] and then using the > using the sweep operator to reduce that matrix. For such an > approach the number of observations does not affect the > amount of storage required.  Adding observations just > requires more time.> > This works fine (although there are numerical disadvantages > to this approach - try mentioning the sweep operator to an > expert in numerical linear algebra - you get a blank stare) For those who stared blankly at the above:  The sweep operator is just a facier version of the good old Gaussian elimination...Andy> as long as the operations that you wish to perform fit into > this model.  Making the desired operations fit into the model > is the primary reason for the awkwardness in many SAS analyses.> > The emphasis in R is on flexibility and the use of good > numerical techniques - not on processing large data sets > sequentially.  The algorithms used in R for most least > squares fits generate and analyze the complete model matrix > instead of summary quantities.  (The algorithms in the biglm > package are a compromise that work on horizontal sections of > the model matrix.)> > If your only criterion for comparison is the ability to work > with very large data sets performing operations that can fit > into the filter model used by SAS then SAS will be a better > choice.  However you do lock yourself into a certain set of > operations and you are doing it to save memory

text: 'In info level SMB_QUERY_FILE_BASIC_INFO
spam: I notice that Samba3 returns aChangeTime equal to WriteTime.  WriteTime = mtime.In Windows
column3: the ChangeTime behaves very similarly to a POSIX ctime (which
column4: contrary to much popular belief
column5: is not a creation time).  POSIX ctime andWindows ChangeTime are both effected when the \"status\" of a file changes
column6: i.e. when its attributes are modified.  In POSIX
column7: this means such things aschanging the mode of the file.  In Windows
column8: this includes such things asmodifying the hidden or archive bits.I have not studied the details of smbd enough to know if changing theattribute bits of a file on the server just plays with mode bits or not.  Ifthat\'s the case
column9: then instead of setting ChangeTime based on get_mtimespec()
column10: it should probably be based on get_ctimespec().Cheers

column25: so I\'m interested > to hear of your experiences & perspective.> > Here\'s my own experiences & perspective:> The requirements are:> > (1) it should be very easy to construct and maintain tests> (2) it should be easy to run tests
column26: both automatically and manually> (3) it should be simple to look at test results and know what went wrong > where> > I\'ve been using a homegrown testing framework for S-PLUS that is loosely > based on the R transcript style tests (run *.R and compare output with > *.Rout.save in \'tests\' dir).  There are two differences between this > test framework and the standard R one:> (1) the output to match and the input commands are generated from an > annotated transcript (annotations can switch some tests in or out > depending on the version used)> (2) annotations can include text substitutions (regular expression > style) to be made on the output before attempting to match (this helps > make it easier to construct tests that will match across different > versions that might have minor cosmetic differences in how output is > formatted).> > We use this test framework for both unit-style tests and system testing > (where multiple libraries interact and also call the database).> One very nice aspect of this framework is that it is easy to construct > tests -- just cut and paste from a command window.  Many tests can be > generated very quickly this way (my impression is that is is much much > faster to build tests by cutting and pasting transcripts from a command > window than it is to build tests that use functions like all.equal() to > compare data structures.) It is also easy to maintain tests in the face > of change (e.g.
column27: with a new version of S-PLUS or with bug fixes to > functions or with changed database contents) -- I use ediff in emacs to > compare test output with the stored annotated transcript and can usually > just use ediff commands to update the transcript.> > This has worked well for us and now we are looking at porting some code > to R.  I\'ve not seen anything that offers these conveniences in R.> > It wouldn\'t be too difficult to add these features to the built-in R > testing framework

column3: I\'d> add Stata to the list).>> Or should we (the users of large datasets) expect to keep on working> with the present tools for the time to come?We\'re certainly aware of the desire of many users to be able to handlelarge data sets.  I have just spent a couple of days working with astudent from another department who wanted to work with a very largedata set that was poorly structured.  Most of my time was spent tryingto convince her about the limitations in the structure of her data andwhat could realistically be expected to be computed with it.If your purpose is to perform data manipulation and extraction onlarge data sets then I think that it is not unreasonable to beexpected to learn to use SQL. I find it convenient to use R to do datamanipulation because I know the language and the support tools wellbut I don\'t expect to do data cleaning on millions of records with it. I am probably too conservative in what I will ask R to handle for mebecause I started using S on a Vax-11/750 that had 2 megabytes ofmemory and it\'s hard to break old habits.I think the trend in working with large data sets in R will be towarda hybrid approach of using a database for data storage and retrievalplus R for the model definition and computation.  Miguel Manese\'sSQLiteDF package and some of the work in Bioconductor are steps inthis direction.However
column4: as was mentioned earlier in this thread
column5: there is anunderlying assumption with R that the user is thinking about theanalysis as he/she is doing it. We sometimes see questions about \"Ihave a data set with (some large number) of records on several hundredor thousands of variables\" and I want to fit a generalized linearmodel to it.I would be hard pressed to think of a situation where I wantedhundreds of variables in a statistical model unless they are generatedfrom one or more factors that have many levels.  And
column7: Iwould want to use random effects rather than fixed effects in a model. column3: Alan Zaslavsky wrote:> I have thought for a long time that a facility for efficient rowwise> calculations might be a valuable enhancement to S/R.  The storage of the> object would be handled by a database and there would have to be an> efficient interface for pulling a row (or small chunk of rows) out of the> database repeatedly; alternatively the operatons could be conducted inside> the database.  Basic operations of rowwise calculation and cumulation> (such as forming a column sum or a sum of outer-products) would be> written in an R-like syntax and translated into an efficient set of> operations that work through the database.  (Would be happy to share> some jejeune notes on this.)  However the main answer to thie problem> in the R world seems to have been Moore\'s Law.  Perhaps somebody could> tell us more about the S-Plus large objects library
column4: or the work that> Spie Bates is doing on efficient calculations with large datasets.>I have been surprised to find how much you can get done in SQL
column5: only transferring summudles of the data into R.  There is soon going to be an experimental \"surveyNG\" package that works with survey data stored in a SQLite database without transferring the whole thing into R for most operations (and I could get further if SQLite had the log() and exp() functions that most other SQL implementations for large databases provide). I\'ll be submitting a paper on this to useR2007.The approach of transferring blocks of data into R and using a database just as backing store will allow more general computation but will be less efficient than performing the computation in the database
column6: so a mixture of both is likely to be helpful.  Moore\'s Law will settle some issues
column7: but there are problems where it is working to increase the size of datasets just as fast as it increases computational power.     -thomasThomas Lumley\t\t\tAssoc. Professor

column3: Bob Rogers <rogers-perl6@rgrjr.dyndns.org> wrote:   >> Surely you are not suggesting that any random \"add_method\" should   >> require creating a new class?  Did you mean \"add_attribute\" (or   >> whatever)?   I did mean that
column4: but only if the class has already been instantiated.    (\'add_method\' can add an additional multi
column6: so it can modify    existing behavior.)Hmm.  If a Lisp implementation ever worked this way
column7: FWIW
column8: it would beconsidered buggy.  It would also make developing Lisp code harder thannecessary
column9: as it is normal to start development of a class by definingit interactively
column16: all withinthe same session.  Lisp uses expect that newly-defined methods will workimmediately for old instances of those classes.   Come to think of it
column17: I also do the same sort of thing in Perl 5:  Atsome time during the execution of my program
column18: I load a file that addsmethods to another class defined elsewhere (though the class may notactually have instances at that point).  It\'s not terribly clean in Perl5
column20: but it can\'t be that rare.   But now that I\'ve brought up Lisp
column21: I should clarify my position.  I\'mstill not sure how I would go about implementing ANSI-compliant Lispobjects for Parrot.  As a result
column22: I have stayed mostly silent on objectsbecause (a) I don\'t know what I want yet
column23: and (b) I assume I will haveto do a lot of PMC subclassing anyway
column24: so that would allow me tooverride whatever doesn\'t work for me.  In any case
column25: Lisp only usesmultimethods -- the first arg to add-method (and remove-method) is ageneric function
column26: not a class -- so I don\'t expect to need add_methodanyway.   So I mention Lisp behavior not because I think Parrot ought to behavethat way
column27: but as a way of explaining why this surprises me.   >> The remove_* operations could stay
column28: they would just   >> throw errors on instantiated classes.   They could
column29: but how often are people going to add a bunch of attributes    and methods and then remove them immediately before they ever    instantiate the class? . . .When the class is cloned
column31: because there are as yet no instances of the cloned class.  So thenremove_* would be useful on the clone.  True?   > Not all languages want to clone their classes on modification.  These   > languages would use their own class PMCs that don\'t clone themselves.   They might not clone their classes from the user perspective
column32: but    internally it\'s the only truly safe way to modify a class that already    has objects instantiated (especially when you\'re talking about remove    operations). Otherwise
column33: you have objects referencing attributes that    don\'t exist any longer in the class
column34: or methods referencing attributes    that were never initialized in the object. The closest they can come is    the option 1) I listed.Note that Lisp uses a form of option 1
column35: where an old instance is updatedto the new class structure at some time before its slots (attributes)are next accessed [1].  I understand there are ways of making thisupdate relatively cheap
column36: without slowing down other method dispatch
column37: butI\'m afraid I\'m not familiar with them.  In any case
column38: it need not be allthat cheap
column39: because it\'s not really needed in production code.   > If one of their classes is passed to and cloned by a different HLL
column40: > their class system will be screwed up/inconsistent.  I\'m not sure how   > requiring HLLs to deal with explicit cloning would be simpler than   > having it abstracted away.  This system is much more flexible.The normal use case for this class-changing API
column42: is toredefine an HLL class definition incrementally by recompiling it.Having one HLL mutate the class of another HLL seems relatively arcane.Are you suggesting that this is a bad idea simply because it can beabused in this manner?   Despite being arcane
column43: and assuming the operation makes sense at all
column44: I would argue that this scenario still ought to work.  If the basicParrot classes support mutation
column45: then even an HLL that normally definesinflexible classes ought to inherit that mutability
column46: unless it doessomething explicit to disable it.  In which case
column47: it ought to disablethe \"clone\" op as well.   The point about abstraction is a good one. It can also be satisfied by    the \'clone\' method/vtable. If a class has a different way of handling    modifications
column48: it can return a modified version of itself instead of    returning a new clone (in those cases where the cloning operation was    flagged as a modification of an existing class).Would the code that does the class mutation need to do anythingdifferent with the result in the \"clone\" vs. \"no clone\" case?  I.e. interms of mutating it further
column49: or doing something to finalize thechanges?   What if the mutated class has subclasses?  I imagine they would needto be cloned (automatically or not) as well?   >> Error recovery would also be easier for explicit cloning; what happens   >> if one of the class-mutating methods throws an error?   >    > I\'m afraid you lost me.  How would this be different?  Could you   > provide some more information?   Essentially
column52: and the automatic cloning fails for some reason? Then you get a    mysterious exception about \"failed to clone class\"
column53: leaving the average    user wondering why it was trying to clone a class in the first place.   AllisonHere\'s another example:  Suppose you change a class definition in such away that several attributes are deleted
column54: and a few more are added.  Ifthat looks like an single operation at the HLL level
column55: even though ittakes a slew of Parrot ops
column56: then you want to be sure that the classmanipulation succeeds completely before replacing the original classdefinition as the one that find_class should return.\t\t\t\t\t-- Bob'

column3: Francesco Poli <frx@firenze.linux.it>  wrote:> OK
column4: this is my attempt to rephrase clause 5d in a form that is weak> enough to be less harmful than clause 2c of GPLv2:>  ~~~~~~~~~~~~ begin proposed text ~~~~~~~~~~~~>       d) If the Program has interactive user interfaces which display>      legal notices
column5: this feature must be preserved in each interactive>      interface that is also present in the work.  In this subsection
column6: an>      interactive interface is said to \"display legal notices\" if it>      includes a convenient feature that displays an appropriate>      copyright notice
column7: and tells the user that there is no warranty for>      the work (unless you provide a warranty)
column8: that licensees may convey>      the work under this License
column9: and how to view a copy of this>      License.>  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~ end proposed text ~~~~~~~~~~~~~What does \"each interactive interface\" mean? I.e.
column10: what delimiters an  interface?Does a program with more than one window have more than one interface?What if it is a web application with several clients? That each open  differentwindows? (This is not specified in the GPLv3 draft either
column11: but I don\'t  thinkit is at all obvious.)Anyway
column12: consider this case:  Program A has a graphical user interface with an \"about\" feature showing  legal  notices. It also has some very clever algorithms in its belly.  Program B wants to use the algorithms
column13: but cares not for the interface of  program A.  Program B has an interactive textual user interface.  (Can the *feature* be preserved when going from graphical to textual?)  Program B extracts the algorithms and uses them
column14: but dumps the interface.  Should Program B preserve the legal notices? Obviously yes.  Now the people at Program B Software first extract the clever algorithms  and distributes them
column17: as allowed by  the GPL.  Then they use *this* distribution in program B. The program they use has  no interactive  user interface at all
column18: and no feature displaying legal notices
column19: so  program B isn\'t  required to have it either.This problem is inherent to linking a requirement relating to an entire  programto only parts of that program (here: the user interface). Anybody can  remove thoseparts and distribute the rest
column20: thereby removing the requirement.Your version does alleviate this problem. Clause 5d of GPLv3draft3
column22: does. It requires that legal notices be inserted if deriving form a programwith no user interface (but not from one with a user interface but withoutlegal notices). It\'s not necessarily the same notices as the original  program
column24: just the default GPL notices./L--Lasse R. Nielsen - atwork@infimum.dk  \'Faith without judgement merely degrades the spirit divine\'  Reproduction of this message

Apr 13
column7: 2007   In late 2005
column8: the Knesset passed Israel\'s first Nazi-era restitution law.The legislation was the work of the Parliamentary Inquiry Committee for theLocation and Restitution of Assets of Holocaust Victims
column9: which had been setup by Knesset member Colette Avital after reports that Israeli institutionsheld bank accounts and real estate belonging to Jews who perished in theHolocaust.   To ensure that no Nazi victims\' assets would be overlooked
column10: the Knessetrestitution law broadly defined property to include real estate
column14: books and artifacts.   Earlier this year
column15: an important provision of the law went into effect - withunintended consequences
column16: thanks to that vague definition of property.   The provision mandated an independent company to locate the owners or heirsof all assets in Israel that had belonged to Jews last known to have been inEurope in 1945. As of January 26
column17: ownership of these Holocaust assetsbelongs to the company
column18: which operates under the lengthy name of the Hevrafor Locating and Returning Assets of Those Who Perished in the Holocaust.Any heirless assets are now to be sold by the company to aid survivors andto assist Holocaust memorial and documentation centers.   Having failed to exclude artworks and artifacts from the definition ofproperty in the 2005 restitution law
column19: the Knesset transferred ownership ofthese assets to the new company - a result that Avital herself admits wasnot intended by the law.   \"During almost five years of work
column20: no one brought up the issue of artworks
column21: because the terms of reference of the committee covered only propertyacquired in Israel
column22: or bank accounts opened in Israel
column23: \" Avital said. \"To thebest of our knowledge
column24: Jews in Europe did not send their art collections toPalestine.\"   This
column26: is a specious distinction. The underlying basis ofrestitution laws
column28: is very simple: European Jewsowned properties before the Holocaust. Through theft
column29: displacement orabandonment caused by the owner\'s persecution or death
column30: Jewish propertieswent unclaimed or became heirless.   It does not matter how the assets arrived in Israel. Whether they weredeposited or purchased by European Jews before World War II
column33: they are all legitimatecandidates for restitution.   The Israel Museum - which received artworks both from donors and from theJewish Restitution Successor Organization
column34: the predecessor to the ClaimsConference - was astonished to find some of its treasures now owned by thenew company. And Yad Vashem could in theory find itself compelled torelinquish artifacts of destroyed Jewish communities on the grounds thatthese pieces of documentary evidence last belonged to Jews in Europe in1945.   Such developments clearly call for a revisiting of the restitution law. Someare already calling on the Knesset to amend it to exclude artworks andartifacts.   Inadvertent as it may have been to include artworks within the framework ofthe new law
column36: it would be a grave mistake - indeed
column37: it wouldcompound the original one - to exclude them by amendment.   One cannot cherry-pick which Jewish properties should be restored. The Stateof Israel should not imply through its legislation that restitution shouldbe limited to bank accounts and real estate and that cultural properties areoff limits. It would send the message that Holocaust survivors are entitledto recover their bank account but not the painting that hung in their familyhome.   Instead
column38: the Knesset should take this opportunity to encourage Israelimuseums to do what every other museum in the world has been prodded to do byIsrael and Jewish organizations: Undertake systematic provenance researchabout their collections
column39: with every effort made to find owners or heirs ofplundered properties.   If the Knesset amends the new restitution law
column40: it should make provisions toretain in museums those Holocaust artworks and artifacts whose owners andheirs cannot be identified. Otherwise
column41: we could face an unfortunate irony:The Knesset-mandated independent company may one day take custody ofartworks and artifacts in Yad Vashem and other Israeli museums
column42: auction theheirless assets - and then give back the proceeds to Yad Vashem and otherHolocaust memorials.   Marilyn Henry is the author of \"Confronting the Perpetrators: A History ofthe Claims Conference\" (Vallentine Mitchell). ------------------------------_______________________________________________MSN-list mailing listMSN-list@te.verweg.comhttp://duvel.te.verweg.com/cgi-bin/mailman/listinfo/msn-listEnd of MSN-list Digest
